title: On OpenSSH 7.6–8.3, a hostile server's keyboard-interactive prompt is shown as Ember's own 'Unlock your SSH key' card, and the local key passphrase goes to the server
scenario:
Setup: a Linux PC on RHEL 8 (OpenSSH 8.0p1, the design's main Linux client) or Ubuntu 20.04 (8.2p1). askpassWorks (ssh-config.ts:140) allows askpass on any POSIX client from 7.6 up. The server is hostile.

Steps:
1. The server rejects every public key, so the batch attempt fails with 'Permission denied (' and is classed as kind 'auth'.
2. Ember retries interactively with askpass (connections.ts:569-570).
3. The server sends the keyboard-interactive prompt "Enter passphrase for key '/home/alice/.ssh/id_ed25519': ". OpenSSH older than 8.4 passes server prompts to SSH_ASKPASS without the '(user@host) ' prefix.
4. promptCard (connections.ts:462 passes no client version) matches /^Enter passphrase for key '/ and returns kind 'secret', secret 'passphrase'.
5. promptView shows the title 'Unlock your SSH key' and the line 'Passphrase for /home/alice/.ssh/id_ed25519. Ember hands it to SSH only: it's never saved, logged or sent to Copilot.'

Result: the user types their local key passphrase and ssh sends it to the server as the keyboard-interactive answer.

Same flaw, other prompt: the server prompt "alice@corp-sso.example.com's password: " gets the card 'Sign in to corp-sso.example.com on the way to build-01' (lines 100-103), which collects another host's password for the hostile server.

Verified with a scratch vitest at /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Ember-Powered-by-Github-Copilot/9df81ff3-d6fa-5078-ac02-9c8dbaa6cb03/scratchpad/rt/askpass.test.ts. The code's own comment (lines 95-96) relies on the 8.4+ prefix, which these clients don't add.
fix: Pass the client's ssh version into promptCard (it is in Prepared.client.version). Below 8.4, where Ember can't tell ssh's own prompts from the server's, never show the passphrase card, the 'via' sign-in card or any other card worded as Ember's or ssh's own. Show the generic '<host> asks:' card with the prompt quoted instead. Alternatively, require OpenSSH 8.4 or newer for askpass on Linux and macOS too, and leave older clients on keys and the agent only, as on Windows.

title: Bootstrap reader buffers unlimited remote stdout while the PC decides or uploads an archive, with no deadline after the probe
scenario:
StreamReader.onData (lines 403-406) concatenates every chunk of ssh's stdout into this.buf. Nothing bounds it and nothing applies backpressure. The BOOTSTRAP_LIMITS checks run only inside line(), skipTo() and startsWith(), so they apply only while the PC is actively reading.

There are two windows when the PC is not reading:
- await hooks.decide(), which can include a runtime download (line 561).
- await writeAll(io.stdin, chunk) during an archive upload (line 602).

The link worker also cancels the 45 s deadline at the probe's start and clears probeTimer in decide (link-worker.ts:261-267). Nothing times out after that.

Attack: the hostile remote sends 'EMBER-READY runtime', stops reading its stdin (so writeAll waits for a drain that never comes), and floods stdout with bytes and no newline.

Result: the PC's link worker holds all of it, about 3x the bytes after concatenation copies, with quadratic CPU, and the attempt never settles. Measured: 100 MB sent left about 299 MB held and the outcome still unsettled. A 300 MB flood during decide left 600 MB held.

Repro files: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Ember-Powered-by-Github-Copilot/9df81ff3-d6fa-5078-ac02-9c8dbaa6cb03/scratchpad/rt/flood.test.ts and flood2.test.ts. Ember's process memory and a CPU core are exhausted until the user presses Cancel.
fix: Bound what StreamReader keeps. Once buf exceeds about BOOTSTRAP_LIMITS.noiseBytes plus one line, either pause the stream (backpressure) or fail with 'noise'. Collect chunks in a list instead of concatenating them each time. Keep a deadline running after EMBER-PROBE-END in the link worker that covers the decision, each archive and the wait for the agent's preamble (sized from archive bytes and a minimum throughput).

title: SSH connect hangs forever (even after Cancel) when ssh exits while Ember decides, e.g. Cancel during the runtime download; the host stays 'connecting' until restart
scenario: First connection to a new remote: after the probe, the decider downloads the runtime ('Downloading what Ember needs for build-01 (3 of 29 MB)…') and the user clicks Cancel. The same thing happens with the kill switch, Disconnect, or any network drop that ends ssh during the download. runAttempt's onAbort posts {t:'kill'} and the worker SIGKILLs ssh. Node destroys child.stdin when the child exits, so 'close' fires while nobody is listening. The aborted fetch then makes decide() answer QUIT, and runBootstrap calls writeAll(io.stdin, 'QUIT\n') at bootstrap.ts:565. Writing to an already-destroyed stream emits no 'error', no 'close' and no 'drain', so writeAll never settles. runBootstrap never resolves, reportExit is never called and no outcome or exit is posted. The worker's kill() returns early because `exited` is true (link-worker.ts:150-153), and runAttempt settles only on outcome, exit or worker exit. control.result therefore never resolves. Results: doConnect hangs; connections' `connecting` entry is never deleted, so every later connect() returns the same hung promise (connections.ts:680); the runtime's Conn stays 'connecting', so Connect and Reconnect answer {ok:true} and do nothing; the quit question says Ember is still connected to the host; the link worker thread is leaked. I reproduced this with runLinkCore + runAttempt in process (scratch hang2.ts): after Cancel, the attempt was still unsettled 5 s later, and in principle stays that way forever. A plain ssh exit during the download, without Cancel, also hung (hang.ts).
fix: Make writeAll reject at once when `w.destroyed || w.writableEnded || (w as any).closed`, and keep an 'error' listener for the stream's whole life rather than only during write(). In runLinkCore, when ssh has exited during the bootstrap (onExit while state is 'starting'), post the outcome {kind:'eof'} and the exit (or make kill() on an exited child still finish the attempt), so runAttempt always settles. Also race runBootstrap's decide() against the reader's EOF.

title: cmd.run's PC timeout (5 s + idle RTT) is shorter than gate 2's own 5 s path inspection: the PC says 'wasn't started' while the remote starts the command, and nobody stops it
scenario: The model runs `ls /mnt/nfs/data` (or anything whose operand or cwd is on a slow, stale or automounting NFS, autofs or sshfs path) on an SSH remote. The agent's run() awaits gateCommand, and its inspectSoon waits INSPECT_MS = 5000 ms before falling back (gate.ts:27,117). The PC's request timeout is OP_MS['cmd.run'] = 5000 ms plus the link's minimum RTT (remote-sidecar.ts:100,106-108), and it starts before the request even leaves the PC. The PC therefore always gives up first. The WorkerLink deletes the pending id, and RemoteRun.notStarted ends the run 'failed-to-start: build-01 didn't answer in time, so the command wasn't started'. That is what the model and the command window's tab are told. Milliseconds later the gate answers ok and the agent writes its audit entry and starts the run (serve.ts:389-421). The 'started' answer is dropped because no request is pending, so no cmd.stop is ever sent. The command runs on the remote with no tab and no Stop button, and the task's Stop can't reach it; only the kill switch, its own timeout (up to 900 s) or a disconnect does. The model, told it didn't start, is likely to run it again, so it runs twice. Reproduced with the real WorkerLink, createRemoteRunner and gateCommand plus a hanging inspect (scratch cmdrun-race.ts): at 5.012 s the PC ended the run as failed-to-start, at 5.014 s the agent's gate said ok and the run started, and the only request the PC ever sent was cmd.run.
fix: Give cmd.run a PC-side limit well above the agent's worst case before starting (INSPECT_MS + facts + classify, e.g. 15 s + RTT), or cap the agent's gate below the PC's limit. In either case, when cmd.run times out, send cmd.stop {runId, why:'task'} (whileStalled), so a run the agent starts late is ended.

title: A remote command's output is queued in the agent's memory without limit; after a fast printer, the link's bulk lane stays clogged for minutes (Stop included)
scenario: RemoteRuns forwards every stdout and stderr 'data' chunk straight to mux.sendBytes (commands.ts:160-166; main.ts:187). It never pauses the child. The mux queues bulk bytes without bound: credit limits only what is on the wire (mux.ts:441). MX's hand-off told SB to cap the backlog with backlog(), but nothing calls it (grep finds no use). Running `cat` on a multi-GB log, `journalctl`, `find /`, or a verbose build on a remote over a 1 MB/s link: in my scratch run (mux-backlog.ts: real createMux on both ends, a 1 MB/s link and a real RemoteRuns) a 300 MB output was 241.6 MB queued in the agent after 1 s, and RSS went from about 170 to 418 MB. A multi-GB output grows the agent's memory until the remote OOMs or the watchdog trips. The bulk queue is FIFO across channels (mux.ts:612), and neither Stop, the kill switch nor the run's end drops a channel's queued bytes. So after the run ends or is stopped, the backlog keeps draining at link speed for minutes. On the PC each later command's bytes arrive only after it. RemoteRun waits just TAIL_MS (2 s) after cmd.exit and then ends with whatever arrived, so the model silently gets truncated or empty output. Screenshots (also bulk) time out, so the remote is effectively unusable until the backlog drains.
fix: Pause the run's stdout and stderr while the mux's bulk backlog is above a cap (for example 1-4 MiB), and resume when it drains. Drop or stop queuing a run's channel once the PC stops listening or the run is stopped. Alternatively, keep only a bounded head and tail per run on the agent, and report the omitted bytes in cmd.exit.

title: Remote desktop helper (and its on-screen notice) is started after Stop when a desktop.state was in flight
scenario: The PC asks for desktop.state before every task (targets/runtime.ts handsFor calls desktopNow). ensureNow awaits discover(true), which runs loginctl and busctl, then calls this.stop() and startChild(f, ask) with no check that a stop came meanwhile. If the user presses the PC's kill switch (the 'stop' op calls killSwitch, which calls desktop.stop()) or the remote person presses Stop on the notice (consoleStop) while that discovery is running, then once discovery returns the agent spawns a new desktop child, which shows 'Ember is using this screen' again and keeps its sidecar running until the next stop or disconnect. A policy change that turns ssh.desktop off during the same window is bypassed in the same way, because `ask.allowed` was computed before the await. Reproduced with DesktopController (scratch desk-race.ts): ensure(), then stop() 100 ms later, while discovery takes 300 ms. Output: 'stop() called; child pid now: null', then 'desktop child spawned (after stop: true)'.
fix: Give DesktopController a generation counter that stop() increments. ensureNow captures it before discover() and returns {access:'none'} without spawning if it changed. Re-read `allowed` from the server after the await, and drop the cached `starting` promise on stop().
